title: Letting nature take over
title_es: Dejar que la naturaleza tome el control

questions.q: How is rewilding different from traditional conservation?
options: It aims to restore natural processes and then step back
It protects only the small forests and wetlands that are left
It removes all animals from an area
It is managed day by day by farmers
questions.answer: It aims to restore natural processes and then step back
questions.why: Dice: to restore the natural processes... and then, as far as possible, to step back.

questions.q: Why are beavers considered a key species?
options: Their dams create wetlands that benefit many species
They eat insects that damage trees
They attract many tourists to rivers
Their dams stop all floods completely in every season
questions.answer: Their dams create wetlands that benefit many species

questions.q: Beavers returned to Britain completely on their own.
How did wolves mainly return to Germany and France?
options: Largely on their own, crossing borders
They were brought from zoos in the east
Farmers released them to control deer
They had never really disappeared
questions.answer: Largely on their own, crossing borders
questions.why: Dice: largely on their own, crossing borders.

options: They control deer populations, so young trees can grow
They keep the sheep away from the young trees in the forest
They attract tourists to rural areas
They hunt the beavers that damage rivers
questions.answer: They control deer populations, so young trees can grow
questions.why: Dice: keep populations of deer under control.

questions.q: What economic benefit of rewilding is mentioned?
options: New jobs in wildlife tourism
Cheaper food for city people
More farmland for young farmers
Higher taxes paid by tourists
questions.why: Dice: wildlife tourism is creating new jobs.

questions.q: What criticism is made about some decisions?
options: Local people are not consulted
They are made too slowly
They favour farmers over ecologists
They cost cities too much
questions.why: Dice: without consulting the people who actually live on the land.

questions.q: According to the conclusion, successful rewilding requires…
options: treating local communities as partners
moving people out of the rural areas
bringing back more predators
limiting wildlife tourism

questions.q: Find a phrasal verb in paragraph 1 meaning 'to stop being involved': as far as possible, to step ___.

task: ¿Debería reintroducirse algún animal en tu región? Escribe 120–150 palabras con ventajas, riesgos y tu postura.
paragraphs: For centuries, conservation in Europe meant protecting what was left: a forest here, a wetland there, carefully managed by people. In recent decades, a more radical idea has gained ground. Known as rewilding, it aims not just to preserve nature but to restore the natural processes that once shaped the landscape, and then, as far as possible, to step back.

A central element of rewilding is the return of key species, animals whose presence changes the whole ecosystem. Beavers are a classic example. By building dams, they create ponds and wetlands that slow down floodwater, filter pollution and provide habitats for fish, insects and birds. After being hunted to extinction in Britain hundreds of years ago, beavers have been officially reintroduced in parts of Scotland and England, where they are now changing rivers in ways that engineers would struggle to copy.

Predators are more controversial. Wolves, which had disappeared from much of Western Europe, have returned to countries such as Germany and France, largely on their own, crossing borders from the east and south. Ecologists welcome them because they keep populations of deer under control, which allows young trees to grow. Farmers, however, worry about attacks on their sheep, and the debate can become intensely emotional.

Rewilding projects also have economic implications. In some rural areas that young people have been leaving for decades, wildlife tourism is creating new jobs, from guides to small hotels. Critics, on the other hand, argue that farmland abandoned to "wilderness" represents lost food production, and that decisions are sometimes made by city-based organisations without consulting the people who actually live on the land.

The most successful projects seem to be those that treat local communities as partners rather than obstacles. Rewilding, it turns out, is not only about letting nature take over; it is also about persuading people to share the landscape.
